title: Spillback cascade: analysis and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working analysis and runbook sketch for the "spillback cascade" incidents observed during the 2025-09-17 production event window. The sequence: overloaded hosts started returning early failures and 503s, the routing layer retried and redistributed requests to other hosts without strong backpressure, which rapidly increased queue depth and memory usage on the remaining hosts, causing host-level OOMs and KV-cache thrashing. The net effect was a cascading failure across the serving pool instead of graceful degradation.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture timeline and signals we used for triage.
- Consolidate hypotheses and short-term mitigations we used on-call.
- Draft a formal runbook for future on-call responders with step-by-step triage and temporary hedges.
- Record longer-term engineering fixes to prevent recurrence.

High-level symptoms observed:
- Rapid p99/p999 latency spikes for text/generation routes (request_tail_latency_p99_ms rose from ~180ms to >2s).
- Host RSS memory climbed steadily then hit OOM kills on multiple worker nodes across AZs.
- KV cache evictions exploded (kv_cache_eviction_count_per_min increased 30x), and kv_cache_hit_rate dropped below 10% on overloaded hosts.
- Batch queue depth and batch_wait_time increased sharply (batch_queue_depth and batch_wait_time_ms).
- Front-proxy logs showed surge in 502/503s and immediate retries (proxy_retry_count).
- Alerts: multiple host OOM and high-retry alerts triggered within 3 minutes of first tail latency spike.

Immediate timeline (concise):
- 2025-09-17 03:12 UTC: First user-facing latency alert (p99 on generation route)
- 03:14 UTC: Host A OOM kill observed; SRE auto-restart kicked off
- 03:15 UTC: Front proxy logged an increase in 503s from host A; client SDKs retried to other hosts
- 03:16-03:20 UTC: Hosts B and C show rising RSS and queue depth; eviction rate jumps
- 03:22 UTC: Host C OOM; cluster-level throughput dips; global retry loop continues
- 03:30 UTC: Temporary mitigations applied (see below)
- 04:05 UTC: Traffic shaping and circuit breaker adjustments stabilize p99 latency to near-baseline

What we collected and where to find it:
- Aggregated logs: ELK index "serving-runtime-2025-09-17-spillback"
- Heap profiles: /profiles/2025-09-17/host-*/heap-heap-*.pprof (s3://redwood-profiles/serving/2025-09-17/)
- Batch queue snapshots from admin endpoints: /admin/debug/batches (attached as /artifacts/batches-20250917.json)
- Proxy traces and sample requests: trace IDs stored in linked_artifacts above and trace collector (jaeger:/spills)

Key hypotheses (ranked):
1) Routing-level retry + immediate redistribution without host load signal caused overload amplification (primary).
   - Evidence: proxy shows immediate retries for non-5xx remote errors; no exponential backoff; retry_count correlated with host RSS growth.
2) Continuous batching config allowed unlimited in-flight micro-batches; when a host's KV cache thrashes, each request causes extra memory churn and temporary allocations, compounding memory growth.
   - Evidence: pprof shows many short-lived heap allocations correlated to batch processing; batch_queue_depth and microbatch_count correlated with memory slope.
3) KV cache eviction behavior is non-constant-time: eviction scans allocate and temporarily increase memory under high eviction rates causing memory amplification.
   - Evidence: eviction GC traces show transient allocations and heavy lock contention during eviction bursts.
4) Front-proxy routing policy lacked a hard per-host concurrency cap or circuit-breaker state that prevents spillback to already strained hosts.

Short-term mitigations applied during incident (what we did):
- Emergency throttling at proxy: set conservative per-host concurrency cap (host_max_concurrency=40) to stop aggressive spillback.
- Disabled client-side immediate retries globally for 600s via feature-flag to reduce upstream amplification.
- Reduced runtime.max_batch_size from 512 -> 128 for affected pool to reduce per-request transient memory.
- Triggered rolling restart of the most noisy hosts after draining (kubectl drain && restart container).
- Increased kv_cache_eviction_ttl to 60s to reduce eviction churn (temporary).
- Enabled tracing for a sample of requests to confirm improved routing behavior.

Commands and quick triage checklist for on-call (step-by-step):
1) Validate alert: check Grafana dashboards (Serving -> Pool X -> p99/p999).
2) Identify hot hosts: query metrics: host_rss_bytes, request_inflight_count, batch_queue_depth.
   - example: curl -s http://metrics-api/query?m=host_rss_bytes|filter=poolX | sort -desc | head
3) Check proxy retry logs for high retry_count and http_503_rate: kubectl -n proxy logs -l app=front-proxy --since=10m | grep "retry" | less
4) Snapshot admin endpoints on top hosts: curl http://hostA:9100/admin/debug/batches > /tmp/hostA-batches.json
5) Collect heap profile: curl http://hostA:9100/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/hostA-heap.pprof then upload to s3 for analysis
6) Apply temporary mitigations (in order):
   - set proxy host concurrency cap via dynconfig (teams/proxy config)
   - flip feature flag to disable client immediate retries
   - push runtime config to reduce max_batch_size for poolX
   - if host RSS continues to grow, drain and restart the host
7) Monitor 5-10m and watch p99 and OOM alerts; revert mitigations only after stable period (30m suggested)

Indicator thresholds for escalation:
- If >2 hosts OOM within 10m -> page SRE lead + serving runtime on-call (pager duty).
- If host_rss_bytes growth > 20% within 3 minutes on >3 hosts -> treat as cascade and escalate.
- If eviction_rate_per_min > 10x baseline and kv_cache_hit_rate < 15% -> notify runtime eng (eviction path review).

Runtime debugging tips / evidence to collect (for postmortem):
- pprof heap before OOM and during ramp (two consecutive snapshots separated by ~60s).
- GDB/backtrace if process crashes with abort (only under guidance from runtime owners).
- Admin batch snapshots (batch sizes, wait times, inflight per-tenant).
- Proxy request traces showing retry fan-out (jaeger trace ids).
- Kernel logs (dmesg) for OOM killer reasons and memory cgroup logs.

Short-term code/config fixes to reduce recurrence (owner suggestions):
- Proxy: implement conservative circuit-breaker that tracks host_rss and inflight requests; avoid routing to hosts with recent high OOMs. (owner: proxy team)
- Runtime: add guardrails in batching to cap in-flight micro-batches per-host and per-tenant. (owner: serving-runtime)
- KV-cache: make eviction GC incremental and avoid global eviction scans that allocate large temporary buffers. (owner: applied-ml/runtime)
- Feature flags: introduce a global "emergency-backoff" flag that disables client-side immediate retries when set. (owner: client-sdk)

Longer-term engineering proposals (for roadmap):
- Add host health scoring combining RSS slope, eviction_rate, and queue_depth; expose to routing layer for informed decisions.
- Memory-reservation pool: reserve a small emergency heap allocator region that prevents immediate OOM on short surges and gives time to drain.
- Backpressure tokens: implement token-bucket style backpressure from runtime to proxy to control accepted concurrency per-host.
- Canary experiments for batching changes with stronger telemetry around allocation rates and eviction churn.

Post-incident action items (next steps):
- [A] Finalize runbook and convert to playbook page in Confluence (owner: Marina; due 2025-10-02)
- [B] Proxy circuit-breaker design doc (owner: Eliot; due 2025-10-09)
- [C] Runtime micro-batch concurrency cap PR (owner: Ravi; draft PR link in linked_artifacts)
- [D] KV eviction incrementalization spike analysis (owner: Jun; due 2025-10-15)
- [E] Postmortem write-up with timeline and root cause once full data ingested (owner: SRE PM; due 2025-10-05)

Open questions we still have:
- Why did the proxy not mark host A as unhealthy earlier? Is there a missing signal or is the health check cadence too coarse?
- Are there tenants or workloads that disproportionately caused eviction churn (long contexts + high-temperature sampling)? Need tenant-level correlation.
- Does the client SDK retry behavior vary by language/version and bypass server-side retry protection?

Notes to on-call responders (practical):
- Prefer quick conservative configuration changes (lower concurrency, smaller batches) over large code rollbacks in early triage.
- Always collect a heap profile before restarting; otherwise we lose the only evidence of transient allocations.
- Use dynconfig/flags for emergency toggles so we can revert without deploys.

Appendix: reproducible experiment (dev environment)
- Objective: reproduce spillback cascade locally with 3-node pool and synthetic load that uses long contexts + immediate client retries.
- Steps:
  1) Bring up 3-node serving pool on dev cluster (k8s namespace dev-spill)
  2) Populate KV cache with warm prefixes using loadgen script (scripts/warm_kv.sh)
  3) Run load generator (hey variant) that issues requests with context length ~2048 tokens, qps ramp to 150, client retries enabled with 0s backoff:
     ./tools/loadgen --target http://front-proxy.dev-spill --qps 150 --context 2048 --retries 1 --backoff 0
  4) Observe batch_queue_depth, host_rss_bytes and kv_cache_eviction_count and repeat with different batch sizes to validate memory slope

Contact list for escalation:
- SRE on-call: pagerduty.com/teams/sre-runtime (primary)
- Runtime eng lead: ravi.patel@redwood.ai
- Proxy eng lead: eliot.kline@redwood.ai
- Applied ML: jun.park@redwood.ai
